action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 0.8 nmol/L (reference <0.5) with raised blocking and modulating antibodies; TSH 0.28 mIU/L with normal free T4 and anti-TPO 380 IU/mL on levothyroxine.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and proximal weakness make generalized MG the leading diagnosis; AChR binding antibody is the first serological test (Jacob 2025, Evoli 2019). Thyroid function is tested in every MG patient and he has treated Hashimoto thyroiditis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 12% in nasalis and 11% in deltoid at 3 Hz, borderline 9% in trapezius, normal baseline CMAP and no post-exercise facilitation.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial and proximal muscles
action_criteria.rationale: Neurophysiology confirms the neuromuscular junction disorder and separates it from a presynaptic pattern; slow-rate RNS of weak facial and proximal muscles is the first study (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mean MCD 62 microseconds in extensor digitorum communis with blocking in 6 of 20 pairs.
action_criteria.label: Single-fiber EMG only if RNS were non-diagnostic
action_criteria.rationale: SFEMG is the most sensitive study but is not needed when AChR antibodies and RNS are already positive; an extra SFEMG is acceptable, not expected.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left MRD1 improved from 1.0 to 3.5 mm after 2 minutes of cooling (positive, at least 2 mm).
action_criteria.label: Bedside ice-pack test of the ptotic left eyelid
action_criteria.rationale: He has fatigable bilateral ptosis, left more than right; the ice-pack test is a cost-free bedside test for myasthenic ptosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Well-defined 3.1 x 2.4 x 2.8 cm anterior mediastinal mass without invasion, most consistent with thymoma.
action_criteria.label: Order mediastinal CT with contrast for thymoma
action_criteria.rationale: Mediastinal imaging is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma, which changes management (thymectomy regardless of MG severity).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 3.20 L (70% predicted, 35 mL/kg), MIP -42 cmH2O and MEP 72 cmH2O, normal blood gas: reduced but above crisis thresholds.
action_criteria.label: Measure respiratory function (FVC, MIP, MEP)
action_criteria.rationale: Bulbar weakness, cough with meals and new exertional dyspnoea call for a baseline of FVC, MIP and MEP to stage respiratory involvement and set escalation thresholds (Lawn 2001 20/30/40 rule).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction requiring a change; statin case reports of worsening weakness noted.
action_criteria.label: Check his medicines before starting pyridostigmine
action_criteria.rationale: His medicines (levothyroxine, lisinopril, atorvastatin, aspirin) carry no interaction that changes management; the check is reasonable but not required.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General consensus guidance on serology, neurophysiology and thymoma imaging.
action_criteria.label: Literature on MG work-up and thymectomy (optional)
action_criteria.rationale: Not a clinical step; optional reference only.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
required_recommendations: Start pyridostigmine 30 mg orally three to four times daily and titrate to 60 mg four to five times daily according to response and muscarinic side effects.

Refer to thoracic surgery for thymectomy of the anterior mediastinal mass (presumed thymoma) once MG is controlled, with pre-operative IVIG (2 g/kg) or plasma exchange because of his bulbar weakness (Sanders 2016).

Start prednisone either low (10-20 mg/day, increased by 5-10 mg every 3-7 days) or at high dose only while he is monitored as an inpatient, because steroid initiation can transiently worsen MG; plan a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT/NUDT15 testing) if long-term immunosuppression is needed.

Repeat FVC, MIP and MEP at least twice daily while bulbar symptoms persist, with ICU-level care if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg, MIP is weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP falls below 40 cmH2O or cough and secretions worsen.
Arrange a swallow assessment before continuing oral diet because of coughing with meals.
Reduce levothyroxine modestly (for example from 100 to 88 micrograms daily) and recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks; the low TSH with normal free T4 reflects over-replacement and does not explain the weakness.

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction; EEG has no diagnostic role here (Jacob 2025).
CSF has no role in MG and nothing in this presentation (normal reflexes, no ataxia, no CNS signs) raises a CSF-informative alternative (Jacob 2025).
FDG-PET is not indicated in MG; contrast CT characterizes the mediastinal mass (Jacob 2025).
Brain MRI is reserved for negative serology and neurophysiology or a central mimic; here AChR antibodies and RNS are positive and there are no central signs (Jacob 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to MG diagnosis or staging.
No arrhythmia or autonomic symptom in this patient; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to MG diagnosis or staging.

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, with thymoma; coexisting Hashimoto thyroiditis (polyautoimmunity)

differential.key_features: LEMS gives low baseline CMAPs with post-exercise facilitation of at least 60%, areflexia and autonomic symptoms; here baseline CMAPs are normal, post-exercise increment is 6%, reflexes are normal and AChR antibodies are positive.
Free T4 normal, anti-TPO elevated (Hashimoto, not Graves); no proptosis or lid retraction; fatigable rather than restrictive ophthalmoplegia.
CPEO has symmetric fixed ophthalmoplegia without fatigability or diurnal pattern; AChR antibodies positive here.
Multiple cranial nerve involvement with fatigability cannot be explained by a single brainstem lesion; sensation intact, no long-tract signs.
MFS is post-infectious with ataxia and areflexia plus ophthalmoplegia; no antecedent infection, normal reflexes, fluctuating (not monophasic) course here.

key_clinical_evidence: Fatigable ptosis (left more than right), diplopia, fatigable dysarthria, dysphagia and proximal weakness worsening through the day: generalized MG with bulbar involvement (MGFA IIb).
AChR binding antibody 0.8 nmol/L above the laboratory cut-off of 0.5 is positive, with raised blocking and modulating antibodies.
RNS decrement above 10% in nasalis and deltoid with normal baseline CMAP and no facilitation; one borderline muscle does not make the study non-diagnostic.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows a 3.1 cm anterior mediastinal mass most consistent with thymoma, an indication for thymectomy.
FVC 70% predicted (35 mL/kg) with MIP -42 cmH2O: respiratory muscle weakness above crisis thresholds, to be followed serially.
Low TSH with normal free T4 and high anti-TPO on levothyroxine is over-replacement in Hashimoto thyroiditis, a coexisting autoimmune disease, not the cause of the weakness.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Free T4 is normal and anti-TPO indicates Hashimoto thyroiditis; the low TSH reflects levothyroxine over-replacement. The ophthalmoparesis is fatigable, not restrictive. Adjust the dose; it is not the cause of the myasthenic symptoms.
red_herrings.data_point: TSH 0.28 mIU/L (low) on levothyroxine; anti-TPO 380 IU/mL
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism or Graves orbitopathy) as the cause of ptosis and weakness.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Nasalis (12%) and deltoid (11%) exceed the threshold; with positive AChR antibodies the study supports the diagnosis and SFEMG is not needed.

sequence_constraints.reason: AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).
Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding antibody positive (0.8 nmol/L), with raised blocking (18%) and modulating (32%) antibodies. Anti-MuSK negative. TSH low (0.28 mIU/L) with free T4 within range. Anti-TPO raised (380 IU/mL). Blood count, metabolic panel, CK and LDH within reference ranges. Anti-AChR antibodies are found in most patients with generalized myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

myasthenia gravis diagnosis thymoma thym.query: myasthenia gravis diagnosis thymoma thymectomy guidance

results.finding: Pyridostigmine is the initial symptomatic treatment; corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy are used when treatment goals are not met; thymectomy is recommended for thymoma and should be considered in AChR-positive generalized MG; IVIG and plasma exchange are used for impending or manifest crisis and before surgery in patients with significant bulbar or respiratory weakness.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425 (international consensus guidance)

results.finding: Thymectomy recommendations were updated after MGTX for non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65; eculizumab is an option in severe refractory AChR-positive generalized MG; methotrexate may be considered as a steroid-sparing agent.
results.source: Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122 (2020 update)

results.finding: Extended transsternal thymectomy plus prednisone improved the time-weighted quantitative MG score and reduced prednisone requirement over three years compared with prednisone alone in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522 (MGTX)

myasthenia gravis diagnosis thymoma thym.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; update Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122) recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma. In the MGTX trial (Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522) thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia over 4 months

social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, 10 pack-years, quit 15 years ago

patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old man presented to the neurology inpatient service for evaluation of progressive bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia over 4 months. He first noticed intermittent drooping of his left eyelid approximately 4 months ago, initially occurring only in the evenings after a long day at work. He attributed this to fatigue and did not seek medical attention. Over the subsequent 6 weeks, the ptosis became bilateral, more prominent on the left, and began occurring throughout the day. He began experiencing horizontal diplopia on left lateral gaze, which worsened with sustained gaze and improved after rest. Three months ago, he started having difficulty swallowing solid foods, requiring multiple sips of water to wash down food. He denied frank aspiration but admitted to occasional coughing during meals. His wife noticed his speech became slurred and nasal after prolonged conversation, particularly in the evenings. He denied shortness of breath at rest but noted mild exertional dyspnea climbing two flights of stairs, which was new for him. There was no neck pain, no headache, no visual changes other than the diplopia, and no sensory symptoms. He had not had any recent illnesses, vaccinations, or antibiotic use. He had been seen by an ophthalmologist who excluded dry eye and structural eyelid pathology. Blood work at his primary care visit 6 weeks ago showed a mildly low TSH, attributed to levothyroxine over-replacement; the dose was not changed. His symptoms have a diurnal pattern, consistently worse in the afternoon and evening and better in the morning.

neurological_exam.additional: Dysphagia reported, difficulty with solid foods. No tongue atrophy or fasciculations. Speech becomes dysarthric after prolonged speaking (fatigable dysarthria). No respiratory distress at rest.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, left greater than right (MRD1 left 1.0 mm, right 2.5 mm). Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze at 45 seconds. Limited abduction and adduction left eye — diplopia reported on leftward gaze. Pupils 3mm, equal, reactive. Facial sensation intact. Mild facial weakness bilaterally. Soft palate rises symmetrically but patient reports nasal quality to voice at end of conversation. Sternocleidomastoid strength 4/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly slow. No ataxia. Waddling pattern on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Language intact. Cognitive function normal.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity weakness: deltoids 4-/5 bilaterally. Proximal lower extremity weakness: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally. Distal strength normal. Fatigability demonstrated — deltoid strength decreases from 4- to 3+/5 after 10 repetitions.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout, symmetric. Plantar responses downgoing bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal throughout. No sensory level. No paresthesias.

physical_exam.general: Weight 91 kg, height 178 cm. Well appearing, speaking in full sentences.
physical_exam.respiratory: Chest clear. No accessory muscle use. Voluntary cough slightly weak.
